summary:
Same-sex conduct between men and between women is a criminal offence in Ethiopia under Article 629 of the 2004 Criminal Code. Enforcement is comparatively rare, but the provision underpins pervasive stigma, harassment and violence against LGBTIQ+ people and drives near-total concealment of identity. Stakeholder submissions to Ethiopia's Universal Periodic Review report penalties of up to one year, with harsher terms under aggravating provisions, while a 2009 academic study of the same legal framework reports a maximum of three years for male homosexuality. Sources differ on the ceiling and the discrepancy is not resolved here.

The absence of any legal gender recognition mechanism compounds that exposure. Ethiopia has neither a surgical nor a psychiatric pathway for changing legal gender, so trans men remain legally women and trans women legally men. A trans person whose partner is of the sex recorded on their documents can therefore be treated as committing a same-sex offence, whatever the relationship looks like in practice. No hate-speech or hate-crime legislation covers gender identity, and there is no statutory protection from arbitrary arrest on grounds of gender identity or expression.

Enforcement is episodic and public. On 10 August 2023 security forces raided hospitality venues in Addis Ababa, shutting guest houses and arresting managers; the Addis Ababa Peace and Security Administration Bureau announced measures against hotels, restaurants, guest houses and entertainment venues suspected of involvement in homosexual acts, and called on the public to report such incidents. Activists documented surveillance, entrapment and rising harassment and violence toward the end of 2023, alongside warrantless residential searches following neighbour complaints and physical abuse during detention.

Non-state actors carry much of the day-to-day risk. In August 2023 an online incitement campaign ended in physical attacks, including a 2 August video calling for gay men to be stabbed and a threat reading "We should find them and kill them." Being outed risks physical violence and ostracism, and ILGA World recorded a 2014 case in which a gay man was denied legal counsel and assaulted by other inmates, with no trial records found. In January 2021 police disclosed the sexual orientation of two people released from detention to their families; one subsequently died by suicide.

Discrimination is documented across education, employment, housing and healthcare, with no statutory protection in any of them. LGBTI organisations cannot register: Article 69 of the Charities and Societies Proclamation bars them as contrary to public morality, and Pride events are not permitted, though national LGBTI organisations operate despite the ban. Same-sex marriage has no legal recognition. Christian and Muslim religious bodies campaign for harsher penalties, the Ethiopian Orthodox Church restating its position in June 2024.
tangentialFactors:
The LGBTIQ+ legal framework sits inside a wider pattern of constrained civic space. US State Department human rights reports for 2010 and 2011 document restrictions on civil society under the Charities and Societies Proclamation, anti-terrorism prosecutions, torture and harsh prison conditions, alongside their sections on the criminalisation of same-sex conduct; those general conditions bear on what happens to anyone detained in Ethiopia.

Periodic moves toward harsher punishment have been floated and withdrawn. In March 2014 the Council of Ministers endorsed a bill that would have made homosexuality a non-pardonable offence, but the government later cancelled both that bill and a planned April 2014 anti-gay rally, a spokesman saying the existing jail term was deemed sufficient. In December 2008 religious leaders, including the head of Ethiopian Muslims and leaders of the Orthodox, Protestant and Catholic churches, adopted a resolution urging lawmakers to ban homosexual activity in the constitution.

The F&M Global Barometers time series scores Ethiopia "no" on every protection axis in every year from 2011 to 2024, indicating no measurable movement in either direction over thirteen years. Parallel constraints on expression are documented too: some media outlets restricted discussion of "LGBTQ ideology" in the early 2010s, a 2008 petition for equal rights signed by hundreds of gay people was blocked before reaching the prime minister's office, and a 2012 conference in Addis Ababa was cancelled after religious groups called organisers "missionaries of evil."

Historical accounts suggest earlier, more fluid arrangements. Research on Amhara and Qemant shepherd boys records same-sex relationships before marriage, and a researcher's account from Nuer society describes a person who changed social status and married a husband with community approval. These are historical observations, not present legal protections.
localsOnly:
Residents carry the burden of the conduct offence in their daily lives. Individuals generally do not publicly identify as LGBTQI+, and a 2009 study found that media and elite discourse constructed homophobia while the church campaigned against homosexuality; female homosexuality was simply overlooked in that discourse, though the Criminal Code covers it.

Detention carries documented dangers for citizens. ILGA World recorded police residential searches without warrant following neighbour complaints, physical abuse during detention and a 2014 case in which a gay man was denied legal counsel and assaulted by fellow inmates with no trial record located. In January 2021 police released the sexual orientation of two detainees to their families, and one of them subsequently died by suicide.

Health and support services are thin and heavily stigmatised. The AIDS Resource Center in Addis Ababa reported that most self-identified gay and lesbian callers, mostly male, asked for help changing their behaviour to avoid discrimination, with many reporting anxiety, identity crises, depression, self-ostracism, religious conflict and attempts at suicide. Stigma linked to HIV status affected access to education, employment and community integration, and in 2019 an anonymous activist told the press that widespread misconceptions blaming gay people for rape deterred young people from seeking services. A small advocacy group founded in 2013 campaigns for transgender people's right to sex reassignment surgery, but no legal route to it exists.

Document markers have concrete consequences. In July 2021 German authorities ordered the deportation of a trans woman of foreign origin holding Ethiopian citizenship; after someone found she was registered as male in her passport and attempted extortion, she had been reported to Ethiopian authorities, held about a year in a men's prison and subjected to physical and sexual abuse by staff and inmates. German officials argued she would be safe because she could "pass" as cisgender, citing the absence of explicit gender-identity law.

Community organisation continues despite the registration ban: national LGBTI groups exist and Pride events are refused permission, while a sexual health seminar aimed at men who have sex with men was disrupted by religious leaders in December 2011 but proceeded at a relocated venue after government intervention.
outOfScopeNotes:
The maximum penalty under Article 629 remains unresolved. The Universal Periodic Review stakeholder submission gives up to one year with harsher terms under aggravation; a 2009 master's thesis gives up to three years for male homosexuality; Outright International describes the offence without a figure. The inventory contains no consolidated judicial reading that settles the ceiling.

No source in the inventory addresses entry, visa or border-screening rules as they apply to trans visitors, including whether passport gender markers are examined on arrival, whether a visitor can be refused entry on gender-identity grounds, or which authority handles such decisions. Nothing here should be read as evidence that such screening does or does not occur.

Similarly unsourced: toilet and facility rules for visitors, availability of gender-affirming care to non-residents, recognition of foreign marriages or foreign gender markers, and any consular assistance pathway for a trans traveller detained in Ethiopia. Whether the conduct offence has ever been applied to a foreign visitor is also not documented in the inventory.

Several claims rest on a single tertiary compilation rather than primary documentation, including the 2008 petition interception, the 2012 conference cancellation, early-2010s media self-censorship, and the 2008 Sheraton Addis ceremony. F&M Global Barometers scores are an instrument's coding rather than a direct reading of statute, and its "no" on every axis from 2011 to 2024 should be read as such. The Outright International country overview carries an update date of 12 March 2026, later than other sources, and its description of the August 2023 crackdown as an official action against "homosexuality" is the organisation's characterisation.
